proposedTitle: Respecting Shared Space: What Happened Next
proposedExcerpt: A week after a serious stairwell sanitation problem, the incidents had stopped. The useful lesson was not the camera footage. It was how we documented the issue, protected privacy, supported staff, and followed up without turning the building into a rumour mill.
notes: Merge the useful follow-up details into /blog/respecting-shared-space, then retire this duplicate URL with a permanent redirect to that canonical post. proposedTitle: The Cooling System Fell Behind on the Hottest Day
proposedExcerpt: The first real heat of summer exposed a cooling problem that a clean filter could not solve. I spent the day checking airflow, calling in the right help, updating residents, and making sure the hottest units were not forgotten.
proposedContent:
The first messages came in before I finished my coffee. One resident said the air coming from the vent felt barely cool. Another said the bedroom had been hot all night. By the time I reached the building, the outdoor temperature was already climbing past 30 degrees and my phone kept buzzing.

A few warm units can be a local problem. A stack of warm units on different floors usually points to something bigger. I asked my maintenance worker to start checking suites while I looked at the main equipment. We wrote down the room temperature, thermostat setting, vent temperature, and whether the airflow felt weak or simply warm. That stopped us from guessing based on whoever called the loudest.

## Starting with the simple checks

I went to the rooftop and checked the condenser units. They were running, but running is not the same as working properly. I looked for obvious alarms, unusual vibration, debris around the coils, and anything leaking where it should not. One filter was badly clogged, so I replaced it. Airflow improved in part of the building, but the supply temperature was still not where it needed to be.

Downstairs, my maintenance worker checked that vents were open and not blocked by furniture. He also compared several thermostats against a handheld thermometer. The readings told us the complaints were real and spread across more than one area. That was the point where I stopped treating it as a collection of suite calls and started treating it as a building system problem.

I have learned not to spend hours pretending I am the specialist when the equipment is telling me otherwise. The superintendent still has work to do, but part of that work is knowing when to call the right trade. I contacted our cooling contractor, described the readings, and sent photos of the controller and equipment labels. That gave the technician something useful before arriving.

## Keeping residents informed

The hard part during a heat problem is that residents want a time, and early in the day I did not have one. I could either make up an optimistic answer or give them an honest update. I chose the second.

We posted a notice in the lobby and sent the same basic message through the normal resident channel: we knew about the reduced cooling, staff were checking affected areas, a technician had been called, and the next update would come at a set time. I also reminded people to keep blinds closed on the sunny side, avoid using the oven if possible, and call the office if anyone in the unit was feeling unwell. Those steps do not repair equipment, but they can reduce the load and help us spot a health concern quickly.

Our custodian filled water jugs for the common room and checked on a couple of residents we already knew might have trouble with the heat. I will not share names or unit numbers. The important point is that a cooling failure is not only a mechanical problem. You have to think about who is most exposed while the repair is happening.

This is also why clear reporting matters. A message that says only “the AC is broken” gives me less to work with than the room temperature, when the problem started, and whether air is moving from the vent. I wrote more about that in [why reporting building issues properly saves time](/blog/no-i-cant-read-your-mind-why-reporting-building-issues-matters).

## What the technician found

The contractor arrived late in the afternoon. After checking the pressures, controls, and temperatures, he found that the system was running but not carrying the expected cooling load. It was not something a thermostat reset or another filter change would fix. He adjusted the system, documented the readings, and identified a follow-up item that needed parts. I kept the exact equipment details out of the resident notice because they would not help anyone, but I recorded them in the work order.

Cooling began to improve gradually. That word matters. A large building does not drop several degrees the moment a technician closes a panel. We continued checking the warmest areas and gave residents another update instead of declaring victory too early.

Before leaving, I made sure the on-call staff had the contractor number, the latest readings, and a list of areas to recheck. The next morning, temperatures were much closer to normal. The follow-up repair was booked, and the work order included every reading and conversation from the day.

I did not solve that heat wave with one clever trick. We solved it by checking the basics, collecting real information, calling the specialist at the right time, and communicating without making promises we could not keep. On a hot day, that steady process matters as much as the wrench work.
notes: Complete rewrite and expansion at the existing slug. It removes invented tenant names, keeps the location and employer private, and adds a practical internal link. Confirm the exact mechanical diagnosis against the real work order before any future production use.

assessment: This is the stronger canonical version of two near-duplicate posts, but it repeats its ending, uses an invented tenant identity, and spends too much time on the individual rather than the sanitation, documentation, staff safety, privacy, and follow-up process. proposedTitle: When a Shared Stairwell Stops Feeling Shared
proposedExcerpt: A bad smell in the stairwell turned into a sanitation problem that staff could not ignore. I had to document what happened, speak to the right household, protect privacy, and make sure the person cleaning the mess was supported.
proposedContent:
Our custodian had mentioned the smell more than once. At first she thought someone had spilled something in the stairwell. She cleaned the landing, checked the garbage nearby, and came back the next day to find the same problem. By the third report, it was clear this was not an ordinary cleaning issue.

I walked the stairs with her that morning. The smell was strongest on one landing, and there was enough evidence to treat it as a sanitation concern. That matters because a shared stairwell is also an emergency exit. Residents, children, delivery workers, and staff all have to use it. Nobody should have to step around bodily waste on the way out of the building.

I asked the custodian to document the location and time, then I reviewed the relevant camera footage. I do not enjoy that part of the job. Cameras can help confirm what happened, but they should not turn every incident into public entertainment. I checked only what was needed, saved the information through the proper building process, and did not share the footage with residents.

## Handling the conversation privately

The footage pointed to a visitor connected to a household I knew. I am leaving out names, ages, unit numbers, and anything else that could identify the people involved. The behaviour had to stop, but embarrassing a family in front of the building would not make the stairwell cleaner.

I contacted the tenant privately and explained what had been documented. I kept the conversation direct. There had been repeated urination in a shared stairwell. Staff had to clean it. Other residents had to walk through the area. It was a health and safety issue, and it could not continue.

The tenant was upset and apologetic. I did not need a dramatic confrontation. I needed the household to understand the effect on everyone else and take responsibility for the visitor. I also explained what would happen if the behaviour continued: further documentation and the next formal step under our normal process.

That balance is a big part of superintendent work. You can be firm without trying to humiliate someone. I have written before about [the people part of being a superintendent](/blog/customer-service-building-superintendent-why-it-matters), and this was one of those days when the way I handled the conversation mattered almost as much as the notice itself.

## Supporting the person who had to clean it

The custodian was angry, and she had every right to be. People sometimes talk about messes in common areas as if they disappear overnight. They do not. A staff member puts on gloves, brings the disinfectant, blocks the area, removes the waste, and cleans it properly. Repeated incidents add work and expose that person to something no one should treat casually.

My maintenance worker helped secure the area while she cleaned. We checked that she had the right protective supplies and recorded the extra work. I also told her what follow-up had happened. I could not share private household details, but she deserved to know the complaint had not gone into a drawer.

We reviewed the lighting and camera view on that landing as well. The goal was not to create a surveillance zone. It was to make sure the stairwell was safe, visible, and included in regular rounds. I added a reminder for staff to report a repeat problem immediately rather than waiting several days for a pattern to become obvious.

## What happened during the next week

For the next seven days, I checked the landing during my rounds and reviewed footage only when there was a reason. There were no new incidents. The custodian said the smell was gone, and the extra cleaning stopped. That was a relief, but I did not turn the result into a lobby victory lap.

A few residents had heard that something happened and asked who was responsible. I did not answer. Rumours move fast in a building, and once a name starts circulating, it is almost impossible to pull it back. Residents needed to know the stairwell was being monitored and cleaned. They did not need a person to gossip about.

We posted a general reminder about respecting common areas, but no photo of the person. If an image is ever needed for internal documentation, it stays within the proper process. Public shaming can create a second problem while you are still trying to solve the first one.

## The part that worked

There was no single clever fix. The custodian reported a pattern. We documented the condition. I reviewed only the necessary footage, spoke privately to the responsible household, supported the staff member doing the cleanup, and followed up for a week. The behaviour stopped.

It may happen again with someone else. Shared-space problems never disappear forever in a busy residential building. What I can control is whether staff take the complaint seriously, whether the response is consistent, and whether privacy survives the process.

A clean stairwell is a basic expectation. So is being treated fairly when something goes wrong. My job is to protect both.
notes: Use this as the canonical merged post. It incorporates the only meaningful development from respecting-shared-space-update, removes the repeated original ending, avoids invented names, and keeps camera handling privacy-conscious. If applied later, redirect the update slug here.

proposedTitle: The Rain Found Every Weak Spot in the Townhouses
proposedExcerpt: A hard rain backed water into several old townhouse basements. Clearing the drain stopped the immediate flow, but the real job was protecting residents, drying the spaces, documenting the damage, and planning for the next storm.
proposedContent:
The rain had been coming down since before daylight, steady enough that water was already pooling along the curb when I arrived. I knew the older townhouses would need attention. Their basements have seen years of repairs, patches, and shifting ground. During ordinary rain they hold up. During a hard storm, every weak spot introduces itself.

The first resident called about water near a basement wall. Ten minutes later, another reported water coming up near the floor drain. By the third call, this was no longer one leaking basement. I opened separate work orders, noted the time and location of each report, and sent my maintenance worker to check where the water was entering.

I am leaving out resident names, addresses, and unit details. The useful part of this story is the response, not who had wet belongings.

## Safety before cleanup

The first question was not how fast we could mop. It was whether water had reached electrical equipment, outlets, furnaces, or anything else that could make the basement unsafe. We told residents not to walk into standing water near electrical sources and not to start plugging in household fans wherever they found an outlet.

My maintenance worker checked the affected areas while I called our plumber. Our custodian brought barriers, gloves, a wet vacuum, and absorbent material, but I asked her to wait until we knew each space was safe to enter. A fast cleanup is not worth an injury.

Outside, water was collecting near the playground beside the townhouse row. Leaves, dirt, and debris had covered a drainage point. The water had nowhere useful to go, so it spread toward the buildings and found the weakest paths into the basements. The plumber cleared the blockage and the visible flow began to drop.

That was the first fix, not the final answer. A blocked drain explained why the situation became severe so quickly. It did not explain away old foundation cracks, tired waterproofing, or grading that may direct water toward the walls.

## Keeping track while everything is wet

During a flood, it is easy to run from room to room and trust your memory later. That is a mistake. We photographed the water lines and entry points, recorded which rooms were affected, and noted when the drain was cleared. Residents told us what belongings had been touched by water, and we explained the normal reporting process without promising an outcome that was not ours to decide.

I also kept updates simple. The immediate source had been found. Cleanup was underway. A waterproofing contractor had been contacted. We would return to check moisture instead of looking at a dry floor and closing the work order too early.

That last part matters. A basement can look fine on the surface while damp material remains behind baseboards or inside a wall. I have seen small moisture problems become expensive mould work because everyone was relieved the puddle disappeared. I wrote more about that risk in [Mould Starts Small, Then It Becomes Everyone’s Problem](/blog/the-mould-problem-dangers-resolution-and-prevention).

## Drying is part of the repair

Once the standing water was removed, we set up proper drying equipment where it was safe and appropriate. We checked the lower walls, flooring edges, and stored materials. Cardboard boxes sitting directly on a basement floor are usually the first things to soak through, so residents moved salvageable belongings onto dry shelving while damaged items were documented.

We returned with a moisture meter rather than judging by touch. Damp drywall, trim, or insulation may need to be opened or removed so the structure can dry. That decision belongs in the work order with clear photos and readings, not in a rushed hallway conversation.

The custodian handled the common cleanup, my maintenance worker checked the building components, and the plumber confirmed the drain was flowing. I coordinated the calls and updates. Flood response works better when everyone knows their lane. Otherwise three people mop the same floor while nobody checks the next basement.

## What had to happen after the storm

The waterproofing contractor could not arrive during the worst of the rain, which was not surprising. I sent the photos, locations, and timeline so the visit would start with useful information. The scope needed to include the foundation condition, exterior grading, drainage route, and any failed sealant or membrane.

We also added the playground drain to our inspection list before forecast heavy rain. That does not solve old waterproofing, but keeping the drain clear removes one avoidable source of pressure. I would rather spend ten minutes checking leaves than spend another afternoon moving wet boxes.

Over the next several days, we rechecked moisture and followed up with the affected households. The drain repair held, the drying continued, and the longer work stayed open until the contractor assessment came back. I did not mark the issue complete just because the sun returned.

Old buildings rarely give you one clean cause and one clean fix. That day, a blocked drain triggered the emergency. Aging waterproofing made the consequences worse. The immediate job was to stop the water and keep people safe. The responsible job was to keep watching after the basement looked dry.

originalTitle: Scooters in the Hallway, A Growing Problem
assessment: This is close to healthy length and has one of the site's more natural openings. It needs a modest expansion, standard Markdown headings, removal of an invented tenant name, less invitation-style closing language, and more concrete fire-route, accessibility, storage, documentation, and enforcement detail.
proposedTitle: The Scooter in the Middle of the Hallway
proposedExcerpt: At seven-thirty in the morning, I was moving an e-scooter out of a hallway again. The tire marks were annoying, but the real problem was access: an elderly resident, a child, or anyone leaving in an emergency should not have to get around somebody's parked scooter.
proposedContent:
At seven-thirty in the morning, I was moving an e-scooter out of the middle of the hallway. It was not leaning against a wall or tucked beside a doorway. It was parked across the walking path as if nobody else used the floor.

My maintenance worker saw me lift it aside and shook his head. He had been cleaning black tire marks from the walls and floor for weeks. The rubber takes more than a quick pass with a mop. He has to use the right cleaner, work a small section, and avoid damaging the finish. By the time one mark is gone, another scooter has come through.

The marks are frustrating, but they are not the main reason I care. A hallway is part of the route people use every day and the route they may need in an emergency. Residents using canes, walkers, wheelchairs, or strollers should not have to squeeze around a parked machine. Neither should firefighters or paramedics.

## A near miss by the elevator

Around noon, a long-term resident stopped me near the elevator. I will not use her name or floor. She walks with a cane and said a young rider had passed close enough the previous week to make her lose her balance. She did not fall, but it frightened her.

She had already seen our notices and wanted to know what we were actually doing. That was a fair question. We had sent reminders, spoken to several households, and watched the problem slow down for a few days before returning. From her side, another notice looked like more paper with no result.

I told her I was reviewing storage options and documenting repeat problems. I did not promise an instant fix. I did promise that the hallway would not become an accepted parking area.

The situation reminded me of [why underground parking cannot become a storage room](/blog/why-your-underground-parking-garage-is-not-a-storage-unit). Different space, same basic problem: one person's convenient storage can block access and create a risk for everyone else.

## Storage has to be part of the answer

It is easy to tell people what not to do. The harder question is where the scooter should go. If there is no practical storage location, some residents will keep choosing the hallway because it is close to their door and protected from weather.

I walked the entrance area with my maintenance worker and measured what space might be available without narrowing the exit route or blocking building equipment. Any rack or designated area would need proper approval, a secure way to lock the scooter, clear rules, and enough separation from doors and travel paths. Charging adds another issue. A storage location is not automatically a charging station, especially when batteries, extension cords, and unattended charging are involved.

I am not going to pretend a rack solves behaviour on its own. It simply makes the right choice easier. Once there is a reasonable option, individual follow-up becomes clearer.

## Notices need specific language

“Please be considerate” is too vague. A useful notice says that riding and parking scooters in corridors is not allowed, explains that hallways and exits must remain clear, identifies the approved storage location if one exists, and tells residents who to contact with a question.

The same message should appear where the decision happens: near the entrance, elevator, and relevant corridor. It should be readable, not buried in a long memo. If the building serves residents in several languages, a simple visual can help.

Before posting anything, I would make sure the wording matches the building's actual policy and the applicable safety requirements. I manage the day-to-day issue, but I do not invent lease terms or fire rules at my desk.

## Follow-up has to be consistent

When I find a scooter blocking the hall, I document the date, time, and location. If I can identify the responsible household through the proper process, I speak to them privately. I explain the access problem, record the conversation, and follow the approved notice process if it happens again.

I do not post a person's photo or turn the incident into hallway gossip. The goal is compliance, not embarrassment. A resident may have a legitimate mobility or storage concern that needs a conversation, but that still does not make the middle of the corridor safe.

Consistency matters because residents notice when a rule changes depending on who is involved. If one scooter is moved and another is ignored, the notice loses credibility. Staff need the same instructions for reporting and handling every obstruction.

## The cleaning work counts too

My maintenance worker should not spend his mornings scrubbing walls because people ride indoors. We added the damage to our records so the time and material were visible instead of disappearing into general cleaning. That helps show the real cost of a problem that can look minor from a distance.

We also checked corners where handlebars had chipped paint and places where tires left marks near doors. Repairing those areas keeps the building from looking neglected, but repairs have to come with prevention or we are just repeating the same work.

I still expect to move another scooter. Building problems rarely disappear after one notice. The plan is more practical now: keep the routes clear, create an approved storage option if the site allows it, use direct language, document repeats, and follow through privately.

The resident with the cane should be able to reach the elevator without watching for a scooter. That is the standard I am working toward.
notes: Conservative expansion rather than a full tonal overhaul. It preserves the original lived-in opening and staff detail, removes the invented tenant name, changes bold pseudo-headings to Markdown H2s, and replaces the generic comment request with a concrete closing.
